This is, off the top of my head, possibly the worst RPG I have ever played next to the first Final Fantasy. 

Never have I seen a game where everything it is trying to do, from the mechanics to simply getting experience and even the turn order is so unbelievably flawed that it tends to all work against itself.

If I went into detail, I would be writing far more than you would ever read, so trust me when I say it's bad.

On top of that, it's miserably boring and the definition of tedious. 

The difficulty starts very easy, but gets pretty tough. I got stuck on a boss who, along with his constant respawning adds, just spams hurtful attacks and wipes me out in seconds. I don't even care to try to find a way to beat him, cuz that would mean having to go through at least 2 more insanely long labyrinths after that, and I can't find a reason why I would want to wade through like 20 more hours of garbage.

I could try grinding levels, but that is folly. Once you hit level 30, it takes literal hours to level up, because despite fighting dozens of monsters, you get hardly any experience. Where I was at, you'd get about 150-350 experience per battle. And it takes, though I have never looked, probably 30,000, to 60,000 xp to level by my best guess. Do the math, that's like over 100 battles. Battles where I quit took 1-3 minutes. More math= hours. 

I could try making a powerful team or whatever, but that requires grinding and more annoying mechanics that don't work or I don't understand because the first hour or 2 of the game is them just throwing tutorials at you completely out of context.

A good game would give you a tutorial when doing a specific thing and walk you through it. This just basically gives you the whole instruction booklet up front, then you gotta hope you remember things when you need to. Or look it up, because why not make it more tedious. I couldn't find some things in the tutorials themselves when looking back, so I had to use the internet, which was far more helpful.

The dating sim is okay, but gets...get this...tedious as well. And the story's for each girl are pretty dumb. They build up a lot as you go along, and the resolve is so anticlimactic, it's sickening.

See? I'm already writing too much, and this was being vague. I could go on for a lot longer, but I must stop myself. Good day, and may you never play this.

Conception II: Children of the Seven Stars is a distinctly unconventional Japanese role-playing game that blends traditional dungeon crawling, turn-based combat, and social simulation into a single, unabashedly anime-styled experience. Developed and published by Spike Chunsoft Co., Ltd., the game leans heavily into eccentric design choices and thematic boldness, positioning itself as a title that prioritizes character bonds and experimental mechanics over strict genre orthodoxy. Its identity is immediately apparent: this is a JRPG that is fully aware of its odd premise and commits to it with confidence, for better or worse.

The story unfolds in the world of Aterra, where monstrous entities known as Dusk Circles threaten humanity’s existence. The player takes on the role of a male protagonist marked by the Star God, granting him the unique ability to combat these anomalies. Rather than fighting alone, he enrolls in a specialized academy alongside seven female disciples, each representing a different Star God and embodying familiar anime archetypes. While the overarching plot follows familiar “save the world” beats, the narrative focus is squarely placed on interpersonal relationships, character interactions, and the gradual deepening of bonds rather than on grand political intrigue or philosophical themes.

At the heart of Conception II lies its most infamous and defining mechanic: classmating. Through strengthening relationships with the heroines, players can perform ritualized unions that result in the creation of Star Children, magical offspring who function as the game’s primary combat units. These children inherit traits based on both parents, allowing for a surprisingly flexible class and stat system beneath the surface-level absurdity. Mechanically, this system replaces traditional party recruitment and character growth, encouraging experimentation with different combinations to optimize combat effectiveness. While the concept may initially feel jarring or off-putting to some players, it becomes a surprisingly coherent progression system once its rules are understood.

Gameplay alternates between academy life and dungeon exploration. Within the academy, players engage in dialogue, gift-giving, and bonding events that increase relationship levels and unlock new abilities. These segments serve as a lighter, more relaxed counterbalance to dungeon crawling, though they lack the depth and complexity found in more refined social-sim hybrids. Interactions are largely menu-driven and repetitive over time, but the charm of the character writing and voice performances often helps sustain interest, especially for players who enjoy character-centric narratives.

Dungeon exploration adheres to classic JRPG conventions, featuring grid-based labyrinths filled with enemies, treasure, and environmental hazards. Combat is turn-based but incorporates positional elements, as players can gain advantages by initiating battles from specific angles. Star Children act as the backbone of combat, with diverse classes such as fighters, mages, and support units offering tactical variety. While the combat system is functional and occasionally engaging, it can become grind-heavy, particularly in later sections where dungeon layouts and enemy types begin to repeat with limited variation.

Visually, Conception II presents a split personality. Character portraits, cutscenes, and event illustrations are vibrant, expressive, and distinctly anime in style, giving each heroine a strong visual identity. In contrast, dungeon environments and in-engine models are comparatively plain, emphasizing functionality over spectacle. This disparity can make exploration feel visually monotonous, even as character-driven scenes remain visually appealing. The soundtrack complements the experience well enough, delivering energetic battle themes and softer academy tracks, though it rarely rises to the level of memorability.

The game’s tone oscillates between lighthearted fan service, earnest emotional beats, and occasional awkwardness. Humor is often derived from exaggerated character personalities and the sheer absurdity of the central premise, which will resonate strongly with some players while alienating others. Narrative pacing can feel uneven, as character events sometimes interrupt the momentum of the main plot, yet these same moments are often what give the game its most memorable emotional texture.

Conception II is not without its shortcomings. Repetition in dungeon design, reliance on grinding, and occasionally shallow social mechanics prevent it from achieving the polish of top-tier JRPGs. Its themes and presentation also firmly position it as a niche title, unlikely to appeal to players uncomfortable with its core concept or anime tropes. However, these flaws coexist with genuinely creative systems and a clear sense of identity that many genre entries lack.

Ultimately, Conception II: Children of the Seven Stars is a game that thrives on commitment to its ideas. It may not be elegant or subtle, but it is imaginative, mechanically curious, and unafraid to be strange. For players who enjoy anime-styled RPGs, relationship-driven progression, and offbeat mechanics, it offers a distinctive and memorable experience. Those willing to embrace its eccentricities will find a JRPG that stands apart from its peers, delivering a blend of dungeon crawling and character bonding that is as unconventional as it is earnest.

I was gonna leave a more negative review - combat and dungeons are just bad, but it turns out there's a funny little turn at the end of Ch.3 which makes me less inclined to say this game is COMPLETELY sauceless. That is worth seeing imo, if you can stomach the poor gameplay.

For a game originally released in 2013 it’s still a decent experience. You can feel the PSVita’s limitations, but if you enjoy anime-style dungeon crawlers and have already played more recently released titles like etrian odyssey this could still be worth trying, even if I wouldn’t consider it one of the best titles available on steam in 2025.

For starters, I want to praise the gorgeous character designs and illustrations by Shinichirou Otsuka, they really enhance the visual novel sections of the game and make them more engaging.

The game’s best feature is the child creation system, which lets you build a party of 9 characters chosen from 30 different classes. You will start with children who have low level caps and limited class options but, as the heroines level up, the cap gradually increases and more options become avaiable, this forces you to keep creating stronger children in order to tackle the harder dungeons. Another nice feature is that certain class combinations unlock special combo skills. Combat features an interesting positioning mechanic: you can place your party at the front, back, or sides of an enemy to gain advantageous attack angles, dodge special moves, or keep enemies separated to avoid stacking AoE attacks against your whole team.

As a negative point I would say that the story is the usual saving the world full of overused trophies, the characters are a bit stereotypical but overall a fun bunch. The dungeons are randomly generated but pretty lazy: the only things changing are the enemies and the backgrounds, but it tends to get very repetitive very fast. The side quests are the typical “kill X enemies” or “find X items”, so they are pretty boring too. Another downside is that every time you create new children, they start again at level 1, so a bit of grinding is always necessary (though as the game progresses you will be able to gain exp quickly).

In conclusion, this isn’t the best game in its genre, but it does have some interesting ideas, and it could be worth a try if you enjoy this kind of dungeon crawler.

Conception II: Children of the Seven Stars is a hybrid role-playing and social simulation game developed by Spike Chunsoft.

The gameplay combines turn-based dungeon crawling with relationship-building mechanics. Players control a young hero known as a “Disciple” who must fight monsters by creating “Star Children” through a bonding ritual with female classmates. These children act as battle units, making relationship management central to gameplay.

Dungeon exploration is structured around grid-based movement and turn-based combat. Battles involve positioning, exploiting enemy weaknesses, and managing multiple party groups of Star Children. Combat is functional and occasionally strategic but can become repetitive due to grind-heavy progression.

Outside of battle, the social simulation aspect mirrors dating sim conventions. Players interact with female characters, increase affection levels, and unlock special events. Stronger relationships produce more powerful Star Children, tying narrative choice directly to combat performance.

Visually, the game mixes 3D environments with anime-style character art. Character designs are colorful and appealing, while dungeons feature varied but limited textures. The presentation is polished but constrained by its handheld origins.

Sound design includes upbeat background music and full Japanese voice acting for major scenes. The tone alternates between light-hearted school life and dramatic, world-saving stakes, giving the game an odd but distinct balance.

Overall, Conception II: Children of the Seven Stars delivers an unusual blend of dating sim and JRPG systems. It stands out for its concept and style rather than mechanical depth. Fans of character-driven Japanese games may enjoy its charm and structure, while others may find its repetition and tonal shifts inconsistent.

"Conception 2" is kind of a hidden gem, at least for those who reminisce for JRPGs from the days of old but can accept a more lightweight and quirky experience. The anime styling, including the use of real animation in cutscenes is inspired, and I love Spike Chunsoft for keeping this forgotten game design style alive. The game's overall set up is strange, as you have the typical "save the universe" style JRPG story mixed with a weird sexual dating sim. The game is not pornographic, but there are animations of simulated sexual positions so I wouldn't say it's totally clean, but even old RPGs like Lunar: Silver Star Story had this sexualized anime element so it's not really anything new for the genre.

This game is based on  PS Vita/DS game so it's more simplified in terms of the game play and the 3D graphics are a little unimpresive, but if you can get past that you will probably find there is a decent amount of variety and complexity to the game play. You pick from 7 women to team up with and "mate" with them to create "Starchildren" which can be varied in teams of 3 out of 30 classes. The labyrinths are based off of the 7 deadly sins cliche. You go into each one, avoid and kill enemies and reach the exit. Along the way there are traps and items, but it's pretty sparse and uninspired. The walls seem like a watered down Kingdom Hearts game but the enemies have their own unique style. You attack as part of two teams and you will quickly notice early on that your starchildren are weak and get pummeled to death easily.

There is a whole second half of the game outside of the combat that involves leveling the city, interacting with the seven women and doing other rote tasks like accepting quests to kill enemies or mating at the church to create new starchildren. You can make the starchildren go independent to level the city, and early on this appears to be an easy way to exploit things to get extra cash and unlock everything on the map. There are dialogue sections at the academy that increase your bond with the girls that allow you to make new starchildren. If you want to 100% complete the game you need to unlock all of the dialogue segments and this is a nightmare if you don't know what you're doing. 

You and the starchildren level up and learn new abilities and while the game seems easy at first, it actually ends up being nightmarishly difficult around the halfway mark. Your starchildren have a level cap that only increases if you make new starchildren when you and your companion are a higher level. At first I hated this, but later on I learned that you could drop them off at a day camp to level them in the background. There's also a leveling exploit with certain goofy looking Pokemon-style enemies that lets you earn 5-10 times more experience than you would normally get, and you pretty much need to use it because you need to be around level 70 to finish this game. Beyond this there are sub labyrinths that have harder enemies and better equipment, and certain items you pick up or pilfer off of enemies will unlock more powerful secret classes. In the end I settled on an Ether Sniper, Dungeon Master and Paladin class because this made my starchildren more balanced and better at dealing damage. You will definitely want to consult a guide because the game is cryptic and hard to figure out but even with that you will be very likely to ragequit if you aren't a seasoned RPG player. Bosses will kill you in 1-2 hits and the fact that the game constantly forces you to reset different classes means you can hit a metaphorical brick wall that makes the game feel unwinnable if you get too frustrated to proceed. 

With that said, I didn't care for this game until the second half and then I grew to love it. I got lost in the quirky variety of the game play and while the character's scenarios are all pretty trite and meaningless, they do have unique personalities and the routine dialogue got less annoying as the game went on. Further, the JRPG-style orchestral music combined with the weird JPOP and the anime style just made for a great presentation. I sunk 60 or so hours into this game and don't regret it one bit. If you're looking for a casual playthrough or something you can skim through and move on I would say skip this one because it's very demanding and will punish you horribly if you don't learn (and learn to exploit) all of the weird game play mechanics.

Basically an introduction to the Persona series for those who never played a Persona game before.

The game spends the first several hours constantly interrupting you with tutorial popups informing you of all the systems, but none of that matters due to how easy it is to walk over enemies. The characters hype up bosses that are killed in two hits to their weak points, and there's no need to engage with the turn delay system or repositioning your squads to take advantage of bonus gauges because fights end sooner if you just deal attack damage. 

You produce better squads if you have higher relationships with the girls, and you level up your base by releasing squad members (children) out into the wild. Relationship growth seems to be limited because you can only engage with 3 relationship events before you need to run a dungeon, but nothing stops you from going into the first room of a dungeon and then immediately hopping out again to refresh the 3 event limit. You can just discard your children immediately to level the city; it doesn't matter if you feed it a level 1 or a level 15 child.

Boring dungeon crawls. Boring combat. The classes of your kids and girlfriends all feel the same because you never have to use their abilities to overcome any great obstacles. I don't feel like I'm planning ahead or strategically creating synergy between my units. The girls are all standard personality archetypes. Good voice actresses, but no surprises in the writing.

[h1]Conception II: Children of the Seven Stars - ¿Estrellas o Estrellados?[/h1]

[h2]Resumen[/h2]
Si alguna vez soñaste con combinar citas amorosas con batallas tácticas contra monstruos, entonces ¡felicidades! Debes ser uno de los diseñadores de Conception II. Esta mezcla rara entre simulador de romance y JRPG intenta engancharnos con su originalidad, pero ¿acaso logra enamorarnos o terminamos pidiendo el divorcio? Vamos a descubrirlo.

[h2]Aspectos importantes e interesantes[/h2]
- [b]Generación estelar de niños:[/b] Si algo no puedes negar es la originalidad en su premisa. Aquí no solo combates, también 'creas' descendencia con compañeras para luchar en mazmorras. Sí, así como suena.
- [b]Diseño artístico llamativo:[/b] Los personajes y criaturas tienen un diseño que, o amas u odias, pero no deja indiferente.
- [b]Combinaciones estratégicas:[/b] Más allá de su peculiar sistema de citas, las batallas requieren una buena dosis de táctica, lo que añade profundidad al juego.

[h2]Aspectos por mejorar[/h2]
- [b]Una historia que flojea:[/b] Entre más juegas, más te das cuenta que la trama podría haber usado un par más de revisadas antes de lanzar el juego.
- [b]Repetitividad al máximo:[/b] Si bien al inicio el sistema de batallas te engancha, con el tiempo se siente más de lo mismo. Una lástima.
- [b]Interacciones algo superficiales:[/b] Para un juego que coquetea con el dating sim, las interacciones podrían haber tenido más carne y menos paja.

I've played and enjoyed a lot of trash JRPGs in my day, but I just can't recommend this one for one basic reason: It is utterly unforgivably BORING. The RNG dungeons are as simple as they can possibly be. Just a series of cube-shaped rooms linked by short corridors. That's it. Every single dungeon looks and plays exactly the same, just with a slightly different skin each time. Crawling through each dungeon is absolutely mind-numbing.

And the enemy types are largely limited as well. Oh, and the combat is brain-dead. Most encounters are easily resolved with basic attacks, and bosses go down quickly by spamming magic spells. After 20 hours, I had felt no particular need to engage with "deeper" strategic aspects, if they even exist.

Plus, the story stuff isn't that compelling either. You have no input into the story, and you're practically obligated to pursue relationships with all the waifus, since you need to keep pumping out bebbies with all of them. The characters aren't particularly interesting, either. Most are just stock archetypes, and only a couple have anything novel going on. Conception II just doesn't give me enough reason to keep playing after 20 hours of ever-increasing tedium.

Basically, the only people I could even think of recommending it to are those who are really really into the harem fantasy and absolutely must play a game about having dozens of kids with multiple women. Everyone else, honestly, even an Idea Factory game would be more enjoyable junk-food gaming than this.

If it were possible to leave a "neutral" review I would. Personally I think the story/characters/romance aspect of this game is GREAT. I love getting to know and slowly get closer to the girls. They're all unique and most if not all of them have engaging storylines (I'm partial to Ellie, Torri, and Serina). I even kind of like the party building aspect where every girl's stats and element differs and they pass those on to the kids. The same job/class child can be radically different just depending on the mother, and then there are combo skills from having certain classes grouped together! It's fun to experiment and find new and powerful skills to use. All that said, however, the game is VERY grindy. As early as two or three hours in, expect to start spending A LOT of time devoted to JUST running through the dungeons (which are all very boring) trying to level your Star Children. And unless you literally pick ONE girl to use for the run (which is inadvisable since some dungeons WILL put you at an elemental disadvantage and that is VERY dangerous), you'll also be grinding the girls' levels too to keep up with the protagonist. You'll be wasting even MORE time repeatedly running through dungeons if you decide to do the sidequests - which for the most part are perfectly fine to skip but you HAVE to do a specific questline to upgrade the girl's equipment, which sucks. ゲーム部分はチーム編成ゲーで、主人公とヒロインに子供3人一組の4チームの組合せを考える事が主となる。
チームは能力が合算されるので、例えば高MPスキルの戦士系とMPの多い魔法職を組合せ、そこに順番を考慮した速さのキャラを入れて調整みたいな事を考える。
子供は基本はヒロインとの愛情度でレベルキャップが決まるので、どんどん入替が必要になるのだが、不要な子供を独り立ちさせると街のレベルが上がるし、弱い敵は主人公の強さによって触れるだけで撃破されるので、最低限のレベリング作業は楽にはなっている。
しかし、ゲームとしては完全に作業ゲーとなり、子供も強いのが出たら入れ替えるだけで愛着は薄く、ヒロインも現在のMAXまで持って行ったら目的の子供獲得優先にならざるを得ない。
子供の職種は多いが、結局、使い勝手の良い組合せは決まってくるので、使いどころの無い職種や特定のダンジョンでの限定的な使い方しかないものも多い。

そもそもの戦闘が意味不明なシステムで、最初、複数の敵が出ても1体を4チームで囲むポジションから始まる。
倒すとやっと他のターゲットへの攻撃になるが、任意で相手を選べず、ターゲット外の敵だけがターン毎に移動もする為、戦略性自体がチーム編成だけに依存する事となる。
そこはあまり面白くない。
また子供の生産に必要なポイントを消費して合身と云う技もあるのだが、これがポイントの無駄なんで、だったらハズレでも子供作ってすぐ独立させえて街のレベルを上げた方が有益。
チェーンだ何だの要素もボス戦とエンドコンテンツ以外は意味のない要素になっているし、後述の様にボスが弱いので要素が死んでいる。

また、元のコンソールのエロ目的ユーザーに合わせたのか、ボス戦の難易度は低く、ザコも通り道だけに厳選して戦えば毎回全力で無傷みたいに進めるし、逆に全滅させていると時間でリスポーンするので、稼いじゃうとすぐにプレイヤーが強くなりすぎる、とても甘いバランスになっている。
エンドコンテンツ的な部分まで行けば、あとはチーム編成の作業ゲーとなるが、そう云うのが楽しくないならやるべきではないかも。
武器防具も強いのは宝箱頼みなんで、必要な数が揃うまで何度もダンジョンを出入りする作業となる。
このダンジョンは移動にダッシュとか無いし、VITAに合わせたっぽい不自由で速さも変えられない視点移動もストレスである。

エロ目的の部分はつまらないし、ポリゴンモデルもVITAに合わせたらしいレベルで酷い。
そもそもヒロインキャラの種類に偏りがあり、PSではロリ系がウケるのだろう、何せ年上もロリ系ばっかだしな。
話も良くあり過ぎる奴で、この系統は最近でもスカーレットネクサスなんかが同じパターンで、これもPS系でウケるタイプなんだろう。

正直、400円じゃなきゃオススメにはしないし、400円でもオススメじゃないとも言えるが、チーム編成の部分はリソース管理型ダンジョンクローラーに通じる部分もあって、そこそこの時間やってしまった事からオススメにしといた。
